speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the 1990s, few thought we could move towards some degree of self-sufficiency in water supply.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But two decades on, Singapore is making good progress on this front and in the process also built up an economically relevant water-related technology sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can do what is needed for security and turn it into exportable know-how.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore faces two other limitations which can likewise be turned into opportunities: food and energy, both of which are largely imported.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First of all, I shall speak on indoor farming, which is a growing form of urban farming where crops are grown in a highly controlled environment, protected from the elements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In indoor farming, environmental factors such as the exposure to light, water, humidity and the temperature are carefully calibrated to create an optimal environment for crops to grow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2013, Panasonic Factory Solutions Asia Pacific opened a major indoor vegetable farm in Singapore in one of its factory buildings which illustrates these techniques.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Panasonic started with 10 types of vegetables in its 248-square-metres facility.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By March 2017, Panasonic aims to increase the number of crop varieties to 30 and aims to supply 5% of local vegetable production, up from the 0.015% in July 2014.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not an insignificant target given that all local farms currently produce only 8% of all the vegetables consumed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While Panasonic's crops are currently grown in a soil-based environment as opposed to soilless methods that have been gaining popularity, the company is looking into R&D to boost yield, including vertical farming which utilises vertically stacked racks for space optimisation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Vertical indoor farming is not completely new in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, the Government has collaborated with local company Sky Greens to develop a low carbon footprint vertical farming system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sky Greens began its commercial operations in 2012 and was able to produce 800 kilogrammes of vegetables daily in 2015.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are still some distance away from the scale of production seen in other countries where more land is readily available for indoor farming.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The world's largest indoor farm in Japan spans 25,000 square feet and produces 7.7 million heads of lettuce a year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has acknowledged the potential of the sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is unclear how much of the Fund was disbursed to Singapore-based companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that there is much more that can be done to encourage local firms to excel in this field.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should recall that indoor vertical farming is a high-tech, knowledge-intensive activity that requires the integration of many different types of expertise.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore, as a developed country with limited land and high population density, offers a good test bed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If economic development agencies adopted a proactive approach of grooming local Singapore-based SMEs to develop leading-edge technology and know-how in indoor farming, Singapore could be producing an even higher share of our consumption needs and developing an exportable sector that could contribute to our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Workers' Party would also like to propose that the Government go beyond what is currently being done in urban farming and develop some of our underground space into large-scale indoor vertical farms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was reported in 2013 that the Government was exploring various uses of underground space.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The then-Minister for National Development suggested that, "We can try to push the boundary of usage   – to experiment, to learn and to evolve practical innovative solutions – so as to prepare for the future." We believe that large-scale indoor vertical farming should be given due consideration for the use of our underground space in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The world's first underground farm opened in mid-2015 in the heart of London, in a WWII air raid shelter 33 metres under the ground.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In London where space comes at a premium, an enterprising firm has found an innovative and sustainable way to grow crops and deliver them to restaurants in under four hours.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The benefits of underground vertical farming are, essentially, three-fold.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Underground indoor farming promises to protect our food supply from catastrophic events, security threats, crop disease and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As for affordability, new technologies have enabled higher crop yields for indoor farming.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sky Greens, for example, has been able to produce at least 10 times more yield per unit of land area versus conventional methods.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The world's biggest indoor farm in Japan has claimed to be 100 times more productive than traditional farms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Certainly, not all our food supply can come from underground vertical farming; there are still price differences but it is moving in a positive direction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The amount of water used in indoor vertical farming has been found to be substantially lower due to the layout of the racks and the implementation of water recycling features built into the system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The underground farm in London uses 70% less water than traditional farming.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indoor farming also reduces shrinkage, which is loss of crops during transportation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The much-shorter journey from the farm to the marketplace also means that the crops remain fresh for longer periods after they reach our shelves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third benefit is developing expertise and IP for our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore is well-positioned to become a global leader in the field of underground urban agriculture.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our local enterprises can be nurtured to not only operate indoor farms effectively in Singapore for the benefit of Singapore and Singaporeans, but also to cultivate expertise in designing, installing, implementing and managing such facilities in similar high-density urban environments around the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That could be an exportation sector for our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I would like to speak of another such sector: renewable energy and in particular solar power generation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Solar photovoltaic (PV) power generation is the most relevant renewable energy technology for Singapore – or one of the most relevant, certainly – given our equatorial location and relative lack of feasibility for other renewable energy sources, such as biomass, wind, tidal, hydro-electric or geothermal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Countries are finding that shifting towards renewable energy enhances energy security and economic stability in the face of volatile global fossil fuel prices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, the cost-effectiveness of technologies such as solar PV technology is continuing to improve rapidly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The solar power sector globally has grown by over 10% a year for the better part of a decade and is now worth over $3 trillion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Domestically, solar power would help to build up industrial capacity and create good jobs within the entire supply chain, from maintenance to operations, to research and development.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, there is an opportunity for Singapore to develop leadership in the deployment of solar power generation in dense urban environments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This could be know-how that is developed, internalised and then exported by our locally based companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As early as 2007, "cleantech" was identified as a key economic growth area by the Government, which led to EDB's Clean Energy Initiative.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, EMA has also introduced a number of enhancements to the regulatory framework governing the interaction of intermittent renewable sources with Singapore's electricity grid.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Spending on solar power is dwarfed by current public spending on fossil fuels.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is no doubt necessary to invest in and upgrade our infrastructure for oil, natural gas and LNG in the short to medium term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, there is room to invest more on solar energy in several ways.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, we are fortunate that most housing in Singapore is public housing, which facilitates the achievement of this goal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In October 2014, HDB began awarding the zero-dollar solar leasing tender, meaning that the full costs of solar PV systems are borne by the PV developers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This initiative was leading to the installation of solar panels at some 5,500 HDB blocks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can be more aggressive here and set a goal to install solar panels on every HDB building roof by 2025.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PUB has been looking into building solar panels on the Tengeh reservoir and Choa Chu Kang waterworks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One that is being built in the UK – that is, water-borne solar panel deployment – is reported to cost about £3.5 million or about S$7 million, and will generate around three megawatt.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The UK deployment covers an area about half the size of Bedok Reservoir, which is one of our smaller reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Solar panel deployments across all our reservoirs and also some available parts of our territorial waters outside of established sea lanes, could contribute significantly to energy production.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Japan has floating solar panels in Hyogo prefecture and is now working on building the world's biggest floating solar farm in Chiba prefecture by 2018.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But they will tilt the balance towards greater energy security, lower carbon footprint and exportable economic opportunities for Singapore-based firms to develop expertise in managing, maintaining and deploying urban solar panels, in the same way that Singapore firms have cultivated expertise in urban master-planning and industrial park design and management, expertise that has been very successfully exported.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Above all, there is a need for us to examine the facts and then set a stretch target for what percentage of energy consumption should be achieved by solar by, say, 2030.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to a recent paper by the Clean Energy Committee of the Sustainable Energy Association of Singapore, a conservative projection suggests that the capacity available for solar generation in Singapore is actually 17% of electricity demand in 2025, far above the expected 7% that would be achieved by 2025 without government intervention.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We suggest that a study be undertaken to assess what can be a feasible target for solar power as a share of total electricity generation by 2030, under both a conservative and a stretch scenario, so that we can debate how much should be invested, where and towards what goals in developing solar power generation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In short, we suggest a more aggressive approach to better exploit rooftop and water-borne opportunities for solar power generation, together with investments in R&D in areas such as electricity storage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are at our best when we apply ourselves to overcoming our natural limitations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Today's uncertain global economy holds challenges that require us to be flexible yet steadfast, nimble and adept, and far-sighted in our approach.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Since the early days of our nation, the Government has made it a top priority to grow our economy and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have to keep this dynamic DNA of being adriot, always looking for opportunities and having a can-do spirit even in the face of difficulties.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: That was how new ideas and possibilities were born and painstakingly nurtured into industries, and became reality.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have to stay nimble and adapt to this changing global environment while meeting the needs of Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With this approach, Singapore successfully grew through various phases of economic transformation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, we moved from the labour-intensive manufacturing era of the 1960s, into skills and capital-intensive industries by developing the Electronics, Chemicals and Precision Engineering clusters during the 1970s and 1980s.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: By the 1990s and 2000s, we had made a strong push into knowledge and innovation-intensive activities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: If Members recall, our first five-year National Science and Technology plan was put in place in 1991.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: More recently, the Research Innovation Enterprise 2020 Plan (RIE2020), recently announced by the Prime Minister, is the sixth science and technology plan for Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Today, we have a competitive manufacturing base with key clusters in Chemicals, Precision Engineering, Biomedical Manufacturing, Electronics and Transport Engineering.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, manufacturing remains a key pillar for Singapore and opportunities continue to be found.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Having said that, we are not standing still but moving forward into new and exciting areas of manufacturing.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We continue to target high-value niche segments and enter adjacent growth areas to leverage on our strengths, our workers' capabilities, our local companies' strengths, knowledge and technology in those areas.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: One example is biologics manufacturing in the Biomedical Sciences cluster.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Today, we have anchored nine biologics manufacturing plants from leading companies such as GlaxoSmithKline (GSK), Novartis, Roche and Amgen.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Likewise, we are building on the strengths of our Precision Engineering and Electronics clusters to develop Space Engineering as a promising sector.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Last December, ST Electronics launched its very own self-developed first commercial earth observation satellite TeLEOS-1.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our local SME Addvalue Innovation Pte Ltd has also developed a proprietary Inter-satellite Data Relay System (IDRS) which is being tested on board NTU's VELOX-II satellite launched in December.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: There are currently more than 150 researchers working on satellites and over 30 companies creating high-value jobs for more than 1,000 professionals in this nascent sector.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will also continue to invest in research and development, innovation and capability development to position our manufacturing sector for the advancement of new manufacturing technologies such as robotics, industrial data analytics and additive manufacturing.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As the nature of manufacturing continues to evolve, companies are incorporating more manufacturing-related services into their business models.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, aerospace original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) are moving beyond manufacturing to provide total support packages (TSPs), where the sale of aircraft or aircraft systems is bundled with a full range of support services such as engine maintenance and field support services.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is an important trend and it presents opportunities for Singapore and our companies to anchor more high-value manufacturing-related services such as R&D, engineering, logistics and maintenance.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These activities, in turn, will add to the vibrancy of our manufacturing ecosystem and further strengthen our innovative capabilities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To stay relevant and competitive, we are constantly on the look-out for new areas and opportunities to grow and evolve our economy.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: One of the ideas is to grow the concept of Singapore as a "living lab", where companies co-develop, test-bed and export new solutions that not only address our country's domestic needs but also generate economic outcomes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: An example, also mentioned earlier by Mr Perera, is our nation's water success.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Opportunities like these can still be captured, if we keep our can-do spirit, inventiveness and relentless pursuit of innovation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, we have the chance to turn the challenges of an ageing population into creative energy and solutions in healthcare.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Changi General Hospital's Centre for Healthcare Assistive and Robotics Technology (CHART) is exploring how to provide accessible, affordable and high quality healthcare even as the workforce and population ages.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To this end, it has set up a collaborative platform for healthcare professionals to work closely with academia, industry and research institutions to develop impactful healthcare solutions using robotics and assistive technologies.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The solutions developed could then be exported to other countries facing similar challenges with an ageing population and workforce.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We are also nurturing emerging industries in the area of lifestyle products and services like sports, the visual and performing arts, design and consumer research and development.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These sectors involving creativity and design have a significant non-monetary value that could contribute to social development, quality of life and the overall well-being of our community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We are aware about international sporting events brought in by the World Sports Group, to the range of top-notch art houses; all these various stakeholders and players enhance the vibrant Singapore city life.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Members would be familiar with Procter & Gamble (P&G).

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I understand that P&G's independent innovation research centre located in Singapore Polytechnic is focused on creating product design and development for consumers aged 50 and above in Asia.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This project is called the "Live Well Collaborative".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Its work is relevant to rising baby boomer Singaporeans whose sophisticated tastes could well spurn a new elderly industry, not just in Singapore but the region.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Turning our attention to clean and solar energy, Singapore is a sunny place and we can make that work harder for us.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: There are ample opportunities to tap solar energy and spread the sunshine into new areas of growth.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In fact, Government-lead demand is helping to grow the nascent solar industry.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It is really taking a whole-of-Government approach to create sophisticated demand.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With HDB acting as the Government's central procurement agency for solar panels, agencies with slightly smaller demand can then benefit from economies of scale and enjoy solar energy at a lower cost.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: At the same time, by aggregating and catalysing solar demand in Singapore, we seek to spur the growth of our solar industry.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The increasing adoption of solar energy will also generate and attract innovation around smart grids and energy management.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I have taken pains to cite the various examples, not just solar but also healthcare, sports, lifestyle, advance manufacturing and so on.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is really to share with Members how we are moving into adjacent growth areas.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In all these, some of the benefits extend beyond direct economic impact and will present exciting potential with room to grow.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They not only address the needs of Singaporeans, but also represent participation and efforts from the public sector, businesses, academia and the broader community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The Member talked about technology for vertical farming.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: MTI has been working with MND and AVA.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We understand that AVA has been engaging farmers since a few years ago.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They have been encouraging the farming community to push the envelope, to adopt technologies and farming techniques that would intensify our land use while also optimising productivity to enhance our food security.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: There was some suggestion about the use of underground space and so on.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As Members know, developing underground space has a cost issue, it could be expensive.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We do need to understand what are the trade-offs and the cost-benefit analysis.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, more studies need to be done to ascertain the best use of underground space.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Amidst our efforts to develop our economy, push the frontier, moving into new adjacent growth areas by leveraging on our strengths, the important thing we need to remember in this House is that the top-most priority of why we do all these is because we want to create good job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Even as we nurture new sectors, we are mindful of Singaporeans with new skillsets to benefit from future job opportunities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With SkillsFuture, Singaporeans have the chance of embracing lifelong learning as a way of life so as to stay relevant in today's fast-changing world.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To achieve this vision, we need the support of all Singaporeans, education and training providers, and employers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, firms that move into new industries play a very important role because they are early adopters.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They play an important role not only in the job creation, but in the learning they can facilitate through internships and professional attachments, as well as the partnerships they form with our schools, Institutes of Higher Learning and Research Institutions for these nascent sectors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: If I could quickly share the example that I experienced myself last week.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The advanced manufacturing sector sets a good example.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The same approach of working together to upskill Singaporeans also holds true for our domestic and social sectors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In fact, the SkillsFuture effort extends to sectors, including Retail, Built Environment and Healthcare.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Ms Low, you have one minute left; please round up.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And by working together, we can all chart a better future for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Perera, we only have 30 seconds left.
